title: Excise Tariff Amendment (2009 Measures No. 1) Bill 2009

divisions.question: That this bill be now read a second time.
That the amendment ( **Senator Cormann’s** ) be agreed to.
That the House of Representatives be requested to make the following amendments: That the requests ( **Senator Cormann’s** ) be agreed to.
That the requested amendments be not made.

Consideration resumed from 16 March. Gavin Marshall Order! The committee is considering the Customs Tariff Amendment (2009 Measures No. 1) Bill 2009 and a related bill. The question is that the bills be agreed to, subject to requests. Steve Fielding Before I move on to the requests by Family First on sheet 5755, senators will recall that last night a request was made to ensure that the money collected through the alcopops tax over the last year is legally able to stay with the government and not go back to the industry. Family First had a position, which was the same position as making sure that the money received for the full year for which it was collected does not go back to the industry, plus an additional six months, as a sunset clause. I would like to test that position in the chamber this afternoon and extend it by moving amendment (1) on sheet 5755, which says that schedule 1A apply for six months after the act receives royal assent. That basically means that the government can legally keep the money from the alcopops tax not just for the last 12 months but also for the next six months. Given that last night the Senate agreed to allow the government to keep the money collected over the last year, I am still honouring my view that I think it should go for another six months to give the government even more time to put in place real measures. I am just testing the will of the chamber here by moving this first request. If this motion fails, there is no use in my moving the rest of the requests for amendments by Family First. I move amendment (1) on sheet 5755 in relation to the Customs Tariff Amendment (2009 Measures No. 1) Bill 2009: That the House of Representatives be requested to make the following amendment: (1) Clause 2, page 2 (after table item 2), insert: | 2A. Schedule 1A | The latest of: (a) 6 months after this Act receives the Royal Assent; and (b) 6 months after the _Excise Tariff Amendment (2009 Measures No. 1) Act 2009_ receives the Royal Assent.

That the committee does not press its requests for amendments not made by the House of Representatives. That the committee does not press its requests for amendments not made by the House of Representatives.
That these bills be now read a third time.
That these bills be now read a third time.

speeches.speaker: Jan McLucas
speeches.brief: The government introduced two bills to increase the excise-equivalent customs duty on alcoholic beverages not exceeding 10% alcohol by volume (alcopops) from $39.36 to $66.67 per litre of alcohol content, effective from 27 April 2008, and to amend the definition of beer to prevent tax avoidance, with the measures aiming to reduce binge drinking among young people and raise $1.6 billion for preventative health programs.

speeches.speaker: Mathias Cormann
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the 70% tax increase on ready-to-drinks was a revenue-raising measure without evidence of reducing binge drinking, and that estimated revenue fell from $3.1 billion to $1.6 billion while consumption shifted to stronger spirits.

speeches.speaker: Alan Eggleston
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the alcopops tax is a revenue-raising measure disguised as a health policy, and proposed a volumetric tax on alcohol based on alcohol content to address alcoholism, citing support from the AMA, Productivity Commission, and other bodies.

speeches.speaker: Mathias Cormann
speeches.brief: The opposition moved amendments to validate the alcopops tax collected since April 2008 and to reduce the duty rate on ready-to-drink beverages from $69.16 to $40.82 per litre of alcohol, arguing the government's tax lacks evidence of reducing risky drinking and is a revenue measure rather than a health policy.

speeches.speaker: Gavin Marshall
speeches.brief: The speaker moved an amendment to extend the alcopops tax for six months after royal assent, arguing the government should keep the revenue for a longer period. The amendment was negatived, and the bills were agreed to subject to requests, with the government committing an additional $50 million to anti-binge drinking measures.

The House of Representatives returned the Customs Tariff Amendment (2009 Measures No. 1) Bill 2009 and the Excise Tariff Amendment (2009 Measures No. 1) Bill 2009 without making the Senate’s requested amendments, and ordered the message be considered in Committee of the Whole immediately.

speeches.speaker: Jan McLucas
speeches.brief: Senator McLucas moved that the Senate not press its amendments and argued the alcopops tax legislation is vital for public health, warning that failure to pass it would reverse a 35% reduction in RTD consumption and jeopardise $50 million in health funding.

speeches.speaker: Trish Crossin
speeches.brief: The government opposed the amendment moved by Senators Bob Brown and Cormann to the alcopops tax bills, warning it would create a $1.6 billion budget hole, give a $1.6 billion windfall to distillers, and allow teenagers to again buy cheap alcopops. The speaker cited public health groups including the Public Health Association of Australia, the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, and others urging support for the original tax.

speeches.speaker: Nigel Scullion
speeches.brief: The government agreed to recommit a $1.6 billion bill vote after opposition Senator Scullion missed the division, while criticising the opposition for disarray and a pattern of poor parliamentary behaviour. The opposition thanked the government for upholding the convention, rejected the criticism, and said it had cooperated fully despite a chaotic government program.
